% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{abstract}
We present \textbf{Fitbauer}, an open-source desktop program written in
Python for folding, simulating and least-squares fitting $^{57}$Fe
M\"{o}ssbauer transmission spectra.
Fitbauer is modelled on NORMOS, the Fortran package that has been a
reference in the field for more than three decades: it adopts its
physical model, parameterisation, folding procedure and constraint scheme,
and it reads and writes NORMOS job (\texttt{.JOB}) files, so that existing
analyses can be carried over directly.
It is, however, an independent implementation, not a translation of the
Fortran code, and it introduces a few numerical improvements (exact Voigt
profiles, double-precision diagonalisation of the hyperfine Hamiltonian,
sub-channel folding interpolation, correct uncertainties for tied
parameters).
The program offers discrete fitting of up to ten components (singlets,
doublets, sextets and magnetic-relaxation lineshapes), hyperfine-field and
quadrupole-splitting distributions with regularisation, and three
uncertainty estimates (covariance, parametric bootstrap and profile
likelihood), all driven by a live simulation of the direct model.
Its agreement with NORMOS has been verified on more than 400 synthetic spectra
generated by NORMOS and on 564 fits of real spectra originally performed
with NORMOS; on four reference compounds the hyperfine fields agree within
\SI{0.012}{\tesla} and the isomer shifts within
\SI{0.004}{\milli\metre\per\second}.
Fitbauer runs on Windows, Linux and macOS, offers its interface in eight
languages and is distributed under the Apache~2.0 licence.

\keywords{M\"{o}ssbauer spectroscopy \and Spectral fitting \and
          NORMOS \and Hyperfine parameters \and Distribution analysis \and
          Open source \and Python}
\end{abstract}

% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

$^{57}$Fe M\"{o}ssbauer spectroscopy remains one of the most direct
probes of local electronic structure, magnetic order and oxidation
state in iron-containing compounds. Its widespread use in mineralogy,
environmental science, materials science and geochemistry depends
critically on the quality of the software used to extract hyperfine
parameters from the data~\cite{Greenwood1971,Gütlich2011}.

Several programs have been developed over the past four decades.
NORMOS~\cite{Brand1987,Brand1990}, with its SITE (discrete sites) and DIST
(distributions) modules, is among the most widely used and cited. It is
written in Fortran, runs under MS-DOS and is no longer actively developed;
running it today requires an emulator. Yet many laboratories hold years of
analyses stored as NORMOS job files, and its results are a de facto
reference.
MossWinn~\cite{Klencsar2013} is a comprehensive commercial package for
Windows. SpectrRelax~\cite{Matsnev2012} handles relaxation and distribution
models on Windows. Moessfit~\cite{Kamusella2016} is a free Qt/C++ program
focused on simultaneous multi-dataset fitting. RECOIL~\cite{Lagarec1998}
and VINDA~\cite{vinda} are further established options.
None of these programs is open source, which limits the reproducibility of
published results and makes independent auditing of the code impossible.

Fitbauer was written to offer a modern, open and cross-platform
alternative that \emph{behaves like NORMOS}: a user coming from NORMOS
finds the same model, the same parameters and the same conventions, can
open his or her own job files, and obtains the same results. Three further
goals guided the design:
(i) complete separation of the physics engine from the graphical
interface, so that every analysis can also be run from scripts or the
command line;
(ii) a framework that makes it straightforward to add new models;
(iii) systematic testing, both internal and against NORMOS itself.

Section~\ref{sec:model} describes the physical model and its relation to
NORMOS. Section~\ref{sec:arch} outlines the software architecture and how
it can be extended. Section~\ref{sec:features} summarises the main
features. Section~\ref{sec:validation} presents the validation, including
the comparison with NORMOS on many spectra. Section~\ref{sec:examples}
shows four reference fits. Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses
advantages and limitations, and Section~\ref{sec:conclusions} concludes.

% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
\section{Physical model}
\label{sec:model}

\subsection{Relation to NORMOS}

Fitbauer's physics was written independently in Python and later reviewed,
part by part, against both the NORMOS executable and its Fortran source.
That review served to verify the model and to adopt NORMOS's conventions
where they matter to the user: the definition of the parameters (line
positions, widths and area or depth ratios), the form of the linear
constraints between parameters, the two-cycle search of the folding point,
and the smoothing matrix used in distributions and its edge anchors. Where Fitbauer deliberately departs from
NORMOS it does so to be more exact, and the differences are documented
(Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).

\subsection{Lineshape and transmission}

In the thin-absorber approximation the transmission spectrum is
\begin{equation}
  T(v) = B(v) - \sum_{k=1}^{N} A_k(v) ,
  \label{eq:model}
\end{equation}
where $v$ is the source velocity, $A_k(v)$ is the absorption of the
$k$-th component and $B(v)$ is the background: a constant, optionally
with linear to quartic terms in $v$ (as the background polynomial of NORMOS).
Each line is a Lorentzian of full width at half maximum $\Gamma$,
\begin{equation}
  L(v;\, v_0,\Gamma) = \frac{(\Gamma/2)^2}{(v-v_0)^2 + (\Gamma/2)^2} ,
\end{equation}
or, optionally, an exact Voigt profile (convolution with a Gaussian of
width $\sigma$) evaluated through the Faddeeva function.

For optically thick samples two models are available: the saturation form
of Margulies and Ehrman~\cite{Margulies1961},
$T = B - C\,(1 - e^{-A_\mathrm{tot}/C})$ with $C$ a saturation scale, and
the full transmission integral, in which the source Lorentzian is
convolved with $1 - e^{-\tau(v)}$ and an optional resonant fraction of the
source is fitted, as in NORMOS.

Spectra recorded with a triangular velocity drive are folded around a
folding point found automatically by a two-cycle symmetry search, as in
NORMOS; Fitbauer interpolates sub-channel positions with a cubic spline,
so that a folding point that is not a half-integer does not broaden the
lines. Sinusoidal-drive data (NORMOS \texttt{TRIANG=.FALSE.}) are fitted
unfolded, each channel at its true velocity.

\subsection{Discrete components}
\label{sec:discrete}

Up to ten components can be superimposed. Each one is a singlet, a
doublet, a sextet or one of three magnetic-relaxation lineshapes. Line
intensities follow the $3{:}2{:}1$ powder pattern or are fitted freely.
For sextets with a small quadrupole interaction the usual first-order
shift $\pm\Delta E_Q/2$ is applied; when the quadrupole interaction is not
small, the static hyperfine Hamiltonian (magnetic field plus an electric
field gradient of arbitrary asymmetry $\eta$) is diagonalised exactly in
double precision~\cite{Kuendig1967}, and the line intensities are computed
from the eigenvectors, either as a powder average or for a single crystal
with a given beam direction.

The relaxation lineshapes are a phenomenological interpolation between a
blocked sextet and a superparamagnetic doublet, the two-state exchange
model of Blume and Tjon~\cite{BluemeTjon1968} (the model NORMOS uses
for Ising relaxation, with optionally unequal populations of the two
states), and a N\'{e}el--Arrhenius model~\cite{Neel1949,Brown1963} for
polydisperse nanoparticle assemblies.

Any parameter can be fixed, left free or tied to another one by a linear
constraint $p_\mathrm{target} = f\,p_\mathrm{source} + c$, which is
exactly the form of the NORMOS constraints.

\subsection{Hyperfine field and quadrupole-splitting distributions}
\label{sec:dist}

For magnetically disordered or nanostructured samples Fitbauer fits
distributions $P(B_\mathrm{hf})$ and $P(\Delta E_Q)$ following the
Hesse--R\"{u}bartsch method~\cite{Hesse1974}: a sum of many sextets (or
doublets) on a uniform grid, with non-negative amplitudes regularised by
minimising
\begin{equation}
  F = \|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{A}\mathbf{p}\|_w^2
    + \alpha\,\|\mathbf{D}^2\mathbf{p}\|^2, \quad \mathbf{p}\geq 0 ,
  \label{eq:tikhonov}
\end{equation}
where $\|\cdot\|_w$ is the weighted norm and $\mathbf{D}^2$ the
second-difference matrix; the resulting smoothing matrix is identical to
that of NORMOS-DIST, including its optional edge anchors.
Total-variation and maximum-entropy regularisers are also available.
The regularisation parameter $\alpha$ is chosen with the L-curve
criterion~\cite{Hansen1992}, which can be inspected and overridden by
clicking on the curve.
Sharp (discrete) components can be fitted simultaneously with the
distribution, and parametric shapes (Gaussian, binomial and the
Voigt-based sum of Gaussians of Rancourt and Ping~\cite{Rancourt1991}) can
replace the free histogram.

\subsection{Velocity calibration}
\label{sec:calib}

By default the velocity scale is calibrated with an $\alpha$-Fe foil,
$B_\mathrm{hf} \equiv \SI{33.0}{\tesla}$, using the published experimental
line positions of $\alpha$-Fe~\cite{Kalvius1969}
(\SI{\pm 0.839}{}$/$\SI{\pm 3.084}{}$/$\SI{\pm 5.329}{\milli\metre\per\second}).
NORMOS instead derives the line positions from nuclear moments; the two
patterns differ slightly in the ratio of the inner to the outer lines, so
that the same spectrum yields fields that differ by about
\SI{0.01}{\tesla}. Both conventions can be selected, which allows NORMOS
results to be reproduced exactly when required.
Once determined, the calibration is stored and reused for every
subsequent spectrum recorded with the same set-up.

% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
\section{Software architecture and extensibility}
\label{sec:arch}

All the physics and optimisation code lives in the \texttt{core/} package,
which does not depend on any graphical toolkit. The Qt interface
(\texttt{PySide6} with Matplotlib) and the command-line tools are thin
clients of \texttt{core/}, so the same calculation can be run
interactively, from a Python script or from a batch pipeline.
The main modules are:

\begin{description}
  \item[\texttt{core/physics.py}, \texttt{core/hamiltonian.py}]
    Lineshapes, component absorption and the hyperfine Hamiltonian, written
    as pure functions.
  \item[\texttt{core/params.py}] A single registry of the model parameters
    (names, default values, bounds and which component types use them).
  \item[\texttt{core/fit\_engine.py}] Bounded least-squares optimisation
    (\texttt{scipy.optimize.least\_squares}), multi-start, constraints and
    uncertainties.
  \item[\texttt{core/folding.py}, \texttt{core/data\_io.py}] Spectrum input
    and folding.
  \item[\texttt{core/normos\_job.py}] Reading and writing NORMOS job files.
  \item[\texttt{core/session.py}] Headless orchestration
    (load $\to$ fold $\to$ fit $\to$ export) used by the command-line tools.
  \item[\texttt{mossbauer\_distribution.py}] Distribution fitting.
\end{description}

This layout is what makes the program easy to extend. A new lineshape or
model is added as a pure function in \texttt{core/}, its parameters are
declared once in the registry, and from there it becomes available to the
fit engine, the interface, saved sessions and the command line. Several of
the capabilities described above (the full Hamiltonian, the transmission
integral, single-crystal geometry, unequal relaxation populations) were
added in this way, each with its own tests, without changing the rest of
the program.

Figs.~\ref{fig:gui-main} and \ref{fig:gui-fit} show the main window
and a discrete fit.

% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
\section{Main features}
\label{sec:features}

\subsection{Live simulation of the direct model}
\label{sec:simulation}

The direct model is always \emph{live}: every change to a physical
parameter ($\delta$, $\Delta E_Q$, $B_\mathrm{hf}$, widths, depths,
intensities) redraws the spectrum and its subspectra at once.
A physically sensible starting model can thus be built by eye before
fitting, which makes the non-linear fit faster and less prone to spurious
minima; the effect of each parameter can be explored interactively, which
is useful for teaching; and hypotheses can be compared with the data
without fitting anything. Simulation and fitting share exactly the same
model. Starting values can also be proposed automatically from the
absorption minima detected in the spectrum.

\subsection{Fitting}

In \emph{discrete mode} the user chooses up to ten components and fixes,
frees or ties each parameter. The fit uses a multi-start strategy (eight
restarts around the starting point) and switches automatically to a
global search (differential evolution followed by local refinement) when
the local fits remain poor. The noise model can be Gaussian or Poissonian.
In \emph{distribution mode} (Fig.~\ref{fig:gui-dist}) the program computes
$P(B_\mathrm{hf})$ or $P(\Delta E_Q)$ on a user-defined grid, optionally
with sharp components, and the regularisation parameter is selected with
the L-curve or set by hand.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{img/captura-distribucion-bhf}
  \caption{Distribution fit of a synthetic spectrum generated from a
           bimodal $P(B_\mathrm{hf})$ at 28 and \SI{48}{\tesla}.
           Left: spectrum and residuals. Right: the reconstructed
           $P(B_\mathrm{hf})$, which recovers both populations.}
  \label{fig:gui-dist}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Uncertainties}

Three estimates can be computed for the same fit:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \emph{Covariance matrix} (default): $1\sigma$ errors from the
    Jacobian at the minimum, $\sigma_i = \sqrt{(J^\top W J)^{-1}_{ii}}$.
    Since the counting statistics of each channel are known, these errors
    are not rescaled by the reduced $\chi^2$, as in NORMOS.
    The error of a tied parameter is propagated from its source parameter.
  \item \emph{Parametric bootstrap}: $N$ synthetic spectra are generated
    from the fitted model with Poisson (or Gaussian) noise and refitted;
    the spread of the results gives asymmetric percentile intervals.
  \item \emph{Profile likelihood}: the parameter of interest is stepped
    away from its best-fit value while all the others are re-optimised;
    the $1\sigma$ and $2\sigma$ intervals are given by
    $\Delta\chi^2 = 1$ and $4$~\cite{Rolke2005}.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Files, sessions and other tools}

Fitbauer reads WissEl \texttt{.ws5} files, single-column ASCII
(\texttt{.adt}) count files and two-column velocity--transmission text
files, and it
imports and exports NORMOS job files for both SITE and DIST, loading the
spectrum the job refers to. A job exported by Fitbauer is accepted by
NORMOS, which reproduces the same theoretical spectrum.
A session file stores the complete state of an analysis (data,
calibration, model and results), so that any fit can be reopened and
reproduced. Further tools include batch fitting of spectrum series with
warm start from the previous result, report export, and command-line
programs that cover the same fits as the interface. The interface is
available in eight languages (Spanish, English, French, German,
Portuguese, Japanese, Russian and Chinese).

\section{Validation}
\label{sec:validation}

\subsection{Internal test suite}

Fitbauer is distributed with an automated suite of 587 tests covering the
physics, folding, the fit engine, distributions, sessions, the
command-line tools and the graphical interface. One module,
\texttt{tests/test\_synthetic\_validation.py}, is organised in six levels
of increasing rigour (Table~\ref{tab:validation}):
\begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{Self-consistency}: noise-free spectra generated with a
    reference implementation that shares no code with \texttt{core/} are
    fitted back, and must be recovered to $\tilde{\chi}^2 < 10^{-6}$.
  \item \emph{Jacobian}: the analytical derivatives are compared with
    finite differences (1\,\% tolerance).
  \item \emph{Monte Carlo pull statistics}: $N=200$ spectra per component
    type with Poisson noise; the pulls
    $z_j = (\hat{\theta}_j - \theta_j^{\rm true})/\sigma_j$ must satisfy
    $|\bar{z}| < 0.3$ and $\sigma(z) \in (0.5,\,2.0)$. This is the test
    that checks that the reported error bars are neither too small nor
    too large.
  \item \emph{Hard cases, physical constraints and real data}: overlapping
    lines, narrow doublets, low signal-to-noise, bounds, and the fit of the
    included $\alpha$-Fe spectrum.
\end{itemize}

\begin{table}[t]
  \caption{Levels of the synthetic validation module.}
  \label{tab:validation}
  \centering
  \begin{tabular}{clrr}
    \toprule
    Level & Type & Tests & Approx.\ time \\
    \midrule
    1 & Self-consistency       &  4 & $<\SI{1}{\second}$   \\
    2 & Jacobian               &  5 & $<\SI{1}{\second}$   \\
    3 & Monte Carlo pulls      &  3 & $\approx\SI{46}{\second}$ \\
    4 & Hard cases             &  8 & $<\SI{1}{\second}$   \\
    5 & Physical constraints   &  9 & $<\SI{1}{\second}$   \\
    6 & Real data ($\alpha$-Fe)&  4 & $\approx\SI{1}{\second}$ \\
    \midrule
    \multicolumn{2}{l}{Total} & 34 & $\approx\SI{48}{\second}$ \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{Comparison with NORMOS on many spectra}
\label{sec:normos-bench}

The central question for a user coming from NORMOS is whether both
programs give the same answer. We addressed it in three ways, using
NORMOS/SITE and NORMOS/DIST (demonstration version 27.01.1994, WissEl
GmbH) run under the DOSBox emulator.

\emph{Synthetic bank.} NORMOS was used to generate more than 400 spectra from known
parameters, covering the cases its manual describes: singlets, doublets
and sextets over wide ranges of $\delta$, $\Delta E_Q$, $B_\mathrm{hf}$
and $\Gamma$, texture, up to ten sites with constraints, thick absorbers,
background shapes, different numbers of channels and velocity ranges,
the full Hamiltonian and distributions. Fitbauer fitted each spectrum
(about 6\,500 parameter comparisons). For the first-order
model the median deviation from the true values is
\SI{2e-7}{\milli\metre\per\second} in line positions and
\SI{4e-5}{\tesla} in $B_\mathrm{hf}$, i.e.\ the two programs compute the
same spectrum; with the full Hamiltonian the medians are
\SI{6e-5}{\milli\metre\per\second} and \SI{8e-4}{\tesla}.
The whole bank is regenerated by a single script; rerunning it with the
current version reproduces these figures.

\emph{Relaxation.} SITE's Ising relaxation was probed separately over six
decades of the relaxation rate and for several degrees of polarization.
Fitbauer's two-state model reproduces the NORMOS curves to $10^{-5}$ of the
peak without fitting the rate, which confirms that NORMOS's rate parameter
\texttt{OME} (in MHz) equals twice Fitbauer's exchange rate. For unequal
populations NORMOS uses a rule that does not satisfy detailed balance;
Fitbauer offers it as an optional ``NORMOS convention'' and keeps the
physical model as the default.

\emph{Source-level review.} The NORMOS Fortran source was compared,
routine by routine, with Fitbauer's \texttt{core/}: constants and line
pattern, lineshape, folding, transmission integral, statistics, the
Hamiltonian, relaxation and distributions. The review confirmed that the
models are equivalent and identified the small differences discussed in
Section~\ref{sec:discussion}. The NORMOS source is proprietary and is not
part of Fitbauer.

\emph{Real analyses.} Finally, 564 fits of real laboratory spectra that
had been performed with NORMOS over the years were reloaded from their job
files and refitted with Fitbauer. The fitted parameters agree with those
of NORMOS to \SI{0.0011}{\milli\metre\per\second} in $\delta$,
\SI{0.0019}{\milli\metre\per\second} in $\Delta E_Q$,
\SI{0.017}{\tesla} in $B_\mathrm{hf}$ and
\SI{0.030}{\milli\metre\per\second} in $\Gamma$, and in 355 of the 503
comparable jobs (71\,\%) Fitbauer reaches the same or a lower reduced
$\chi^2$.

\section{Application examples}
\label{sec:examples}

We illustrate the results on four reference spectra included with the
program: $\alpha$-Fe, hematite ($\alpha$-Fe$_2$O$_3$), siderite
(FeCO$_3$) and magnetite (Fe$_3$O$_4$). All consist of 512 channels
recorded with a triangular drive and
$V_\mathrm{max} \approx \SI{12.0}{\milli\metre\per\second}$, and were
fitted with a single sextet ($\alpha$-Fe, hematite), a doublet (siderite)
and two sextets (magnetite). Fig.~\ref{fig:reference-fits} shows the fits.

The same four spectra were fitted with NORMOS/SITE starting from the same
models. Table~\ref{tab:comparison} and Fig.~\ref{fig:normos-comparison}
compare the results. The largest differences are \SI{0.012}{\tesla} in
$B_\mathrm{hf}$, \SI{0.004}{\milli\metre\per\second} in $\delta$,
\SI{0.001}{\milli\metre\per\second} in $|\Delta E_Q|$ and
\SI{0.007}{\milli\metre\per\second} in $\Gamma$, comparable to the
statistical uncertainties of the fits. They arise from the different
folding (NORMOS sums whole channels around its folding point, Fitbauer
interpolates) and from the background model (constant in NORMOS, with a
linear slope in Fitbauer). The reduced $\chi^2$ values are also close; they
are not strictly comparable because NORMOS normalises by the data and uses
one degree of freedom less.
For siderite the sign of $\Delta E_Q$ differs only by convention: both
programs give the same line positions.

           $B_\mathrm{hf}^\mathrm{B}=\SI{46.1}{\tesla}$;
           $\tilde{\chi}^2=0.96$.}
  \label{fig:magnetite}
\end{figure}

% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{Differences from NORMOS}

Fitbauer reproduces NORMOS where NORMOS is exact, and departs from it in a
few places where a more accurate calculation is now inexpensive:
\begin{itemize}
  \item Voigt lines are computed exactly from the Faddeeva function rather
    than with the pseudo-Voigt approximation used by SITE.
  \item The hyperfine Hamiltonian is diagonalised with a Hermitian solver
    in double precision. SITE uses a general complex solver in single
    precision, whose eigenvectors are not orthonormalised; its deviation
    grows with the mixing of states.
  \item Folding interpolates sub-channel positions, so that the folding
    point need not be a half-integer and lines are not broadened.
  \item The uncertainty of a tied parameter is propagated with the
    multiplicative factor of the constraint. In NORMOS the additive
    constant is used instead, so that a purely multiplicative constraint
    is reported with zero error.
\end{itemize}
Each of these differences is small for typical spectra, as the comparisons
of Sections~\ref{sec:normos-bench} and \ref{sec:examples} show.

\subsection{Advantages}

Being open source and built on widely used Python packages (NumPy, SciPy,
Matplotlib, PySide6), Fitbauer can be installed on any current operating
system and its computational environment reproduced exactly, which matters
for the reproducibility of published results~\cite{Peng2011}. NORMOS users
can migrate without redoing their work, thanks to the job-file
compatibility. The program adds profile-likelihood and bootstrap
uncertainties, a live simulation of the model and a scriptable interface.

\subsection{Current limitations}

Some NORMOS-DIST options are not yet available, notably the Czjzek
(Le Ca\"{e}r) and Billard--Chamberod distributions.
Multipolar M1+E2 mixing, irrelevant for $^{57}$Fe, is not implemented, and
neither are other M\"{o}ssbauer isotopes. Conversion-electron and
backscattering geometries, NORMOS's spherical relaxation model and
relaxation between more than two states are also absent. Thanks to the modular design of Section~\ref{sec:arch}, these
are natural targets for future development.

\section{Conclusions}
\label{sec:conclusions}

Fitbauer is an open-source Python program for $^{57}$Fe M\"{o}ssbauer
spectral fitting that follows the physical model and conventions of
NORMOS, reads and writes its job files, and gives the same results:
on more than 400 synthetic spectra generated by NORMOS, on 564 real analyses
originally performed with it, and on four reference compounds, where the
hyperfine fields agree within \SI{0.012}{\tesla} and the isomer shifts
within \SI{0.004}{\milli\metre\per\second}.
On this common basis it adds a live simulation of the model, a modern
cross-platform interface in eight languages, command-line and scripting
access, three uncertainty estimates and an extensive automated test
suite, and its modular design makes new models straightforward to add.

The program, example spectra, calibration templates and a user manual
are freely available at \url{https://github.com/sullymike/Fitbauer}
and archived at Zenodo~\cite{FitbauerZenodo}.
